574.t: Kelly's blues and the Three Sixes
574.s: Kelly was best on blues, including his own Three Sixes; Robinson played his last job with him.
574.q: How many numbers? Well he used to play different numbers but Chris had several blues there. He used to have blues there. He used to have blues there. I don't get how they go but he used to call it the three sixes.

574.t: Kelly's last job, death and Ironton origins
574.s: Kelly died of a heart condition at about 38; he came from Ironton below Magnolia with Sonny Henry and Jim Robinson.
574.q: In McDonnellville. Up in McDonnellville. Yeah. Couldn't walk from near to that door unless he had to stop. He was really sick? Yeah, the wind was just that short. His heart was bad. The heart just gave out on him.

574.s: Robinson says Kelly resembled him, about five foot ten and heavy, unlike small Buddy Petit and Rene.
574.q: Oh, now that's the little, that was the little man. Buddy Petit and Rene. Yeah. Them was little fellas.

574.t: Kelly's temperament, handling money and his gold cornet
574.s: Kelly was likeable but spent deposits on drink, so Robinson collected his own; Kelly kept pawning his small gold cornet.
574.q: Well, he was kind of hard headed, but he could be easy to conquer down. Yeah. Cause I used to conquer him plenty of times. But one thing I didn't like about him, you used to fool with your money so much. Yeah. In them days you always sign a contract and they give you a deposit. Oh yeah, I've heard…

574.t: Chris Kelly's appearance and barrelhouse style
574.s: Kelly was dark brown, a poor dresser, and played barrelhouse music with mutes.
574.q: Oh, he was a kind of dark brown kid fellow. Well he didn't dress so well. He was really badass already.

574.t: Kid Howard's resemblance to Chris Kelly
574.s: Howard started as a drummer and then played trumpet like Kelly; later he copied Armstrong.
574.q: He'd be able to play just like Chris Kelly. But, you're right by and Margetts, Amit, Payton, Lewis and other different fellas, I guess that would spoil his lick. Hmm. Howard was a pretty good trumpet player.

574.s: Kelly swung better than Rene, rocking on his toes; Robinson filled in behind him.
574.q: It seems to me Chris had a better swing in Rene. Chris had, what do you call that good swing? Really got him stopping. Yeah. He looked like I could look at him. No, he'd be sitting on your feet. He started to rock back on his toes. Yeah.

574.t: Chris Kelly's band and its musicians
574.s: Robinson played with Kelly longer than any band; members included Mealy Bong, Peter Patton, Marrero bass, and drummer Faiso.
574.q: Mealy Bong that was one of his old... Yeah, we know him. ...clanet players. And then Peter Patton used to play banjo and then Marrero boys one named Lowndes he playing bass. Oh yeah. He's still living, he's still around. Yeah. And Faiso drummer, well he played drum with us some. We had Big Willie…

875.t: Chris Kelly's band and his wah-wah cornet
875.s: Chris Kelly played parties for all kinds of audiences; his speciality was Careless Love with the wah-wah mute.
875.q: Well he played like the rest of the bands. He was a named band and he was good, his style of playing. He played for a lot of Italian people, Italian halls, but mostly for colored. See he wasn't particular about the way he played, as long as he was playing.

875.t: Playing a Chris Kelly record and discussing his solos
875.s: A record of Careless Love is played; Howard describes Chris's wah-wah solos and bands with featured soloists.
875.q: And he'd play that solo like that. But he'd have that wah-wah with that little mute in it. Take that. Take that. Mm-hm. I'm still out of tape.

875.t: Time with Chris Kelly and his band members
875.s: Howard worked side jobs with Chris, later took Sam Morgan's place; he names Chris's drummer and sidemen.
875.q: And I played, after I started playing the trumpet, I played a lot of times with him. And when Sam died I'd taken his place quite a while with Izil Muggenbaum. I still moved up from second to first and I played the second.

875.t: Subbing for Chris Kelly and taking over his jobs
875.s: Chris sent Howard to jobs under his name; Howard copied his repertoire and gradually gained his own name.
875.q: Well Chris, you know, it'd take more than one job and so forth like that and he'd go someplace and make up something and it still would be Chris' name and not have three or four jobs at that particular night.

875.t: Playing like Chris Kelly: Careless Love and the mute
875.s: Howard says he once played just like Kelly with the mute and wah-wah, and describes how Kelly started Careless Love.
875.q: Well, when I first started and got the band together, I used to play exactly like he played with the mute. I had the wah-wah and everything, and all the time he could tell the difference. When they'd come into the hall, because the Al Jays and all the people was crazy about Chris, and he used to…

875.s: They discuss whether Kelly played for rougher crowds or society dates; Howard says he played many white dances and everywhere else.
875.q: Well no, I don't think he made connection that kind of way because they kept him so busy with those kind of people which you may see. And other words, money, money, and he first come for his soil. Yeah. You see.

300.t: Chris Kelly's playing and where they worked
300.s: Allen links the blues to Chris Kelly; Humphrey praises his style, tone and mutes and lists halls they played.
300.q: He had a style of his own. Yes. Hard-working man. Wonderful tone. He was just a all around good jazz trumpet bell. Awesome. He didn't overdo nothing. Awesome. He used various kinds of mutes. Yeah. Whereabouts would you play with him? Oh, we played all over Louisiana. Different places, lots of…

300.t: Playing with Johnny Brown's band and Chris Kelly
300.s: Humphrey recalls working with Johnny Brown's band, Chris Kelly and Mealy Barnes, and the pressure rival players put on Kelly.
300.q: Yeah, Harrison. Harrison. Harrison Bowen. Yeah. See, cause he was a boilermaker, see? Mm-hmm. And last time he had to work overtime there, he was, you know, working for the railroad.

300.t: How Chris Kelly won bucking contests with his plunger mute
300.s: Humphrey describes Chris Kelly's blues playing, his rubber mute, Leroy Evans' timekeeping and the numbers Kelly played.
300.q: Oh, he played, I'mma tell you, man. That guy, he was a good first-style guy. He played sweet numbers. He stayed at now. Oh, he had something to run him with, no? Mm-hmm. Yeah, man. He could play the blues better than any, any trumpet play any time. Mm-hmm. Lee Codden was a blues player. Mm-hmm.…

300.t: Kelly's Careless Love and how Chris Kelly's band handled keys
300.s: Humphrey explains Chris Kelly's practice of calling keys, fade-outs, dancing rhythm and modulation compared to reading music.
300.q: Yeah, that's Kellis' love. But now, you see, what we've been playing, you know, we play a certain amount of chorus and everything. Called the band down, Saw. They'd break that wah-wah music, you know, that rubber plunged.

300.t: Chris Kelly's double-booking and the decline of his band
300.s: Humphrey criticizes Chris Kelly for sending substitutes to dates and how other bands competed for his work.
300.q: He made a good reputation over there. After he... I had Buddy message bandit the same as Chris did. Chris had a line of work around him, man. He was working, exactly, every night. Five nights every week, sometimes, every night. They take them double dates. Mm-hmm. All right, now.

128.t: What Chris Kelly wore on jobs
128.s: Jim and Percy say Chris Kelly wore ordinary black clothes and bad shoes, and was a blues man.
128.q: Chris did have bad shoes. With that question, Doc, he sure did. Because when Faye saw that time, him and Black Banner had that humbug about tuxedo suits and all that. Chris was a man that's not like to drink, you know. He was a good blues man and didn't wear too much fancy clothes, you know. No,…

128.t: Chris Kelly: age, death and early musical life
128.s: Robinson knew Chris Kelly from home; he died in 1928 and was a fine trumpet player.
128.q: Oh, me and Chris come from the same home. He got on the Chris all my life. You know, I was like, Christmas. Older than what I was, Christmas was my brother Sam. He was there. How old would Sam be? My brother Sam would be, he said it would be 73 other days. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. A couple years older than…

128.t: Subbing for Harrison Barnes in Chris Kelly's band
128.s: Robinson filled in for welder Harrison Barnes in Chris Kelly's band, and traces where Sonny Henry played afterward.
128.q: Who me? No, no, no. I never remember Chris's band. I always remember Chris's band like when someone played, Harrison Bourne was working over at, in the shop, moving out of here. In the shop with a well-tooled, with a bottle of tubes. And when Harrison would get off to play, he'd say, Chris come get…

128.t: Robinson's country ragtime band with Chris Kelly
128.s: Robinson played guitar for country dances with Chris, his brothers, Little Jim and a drummer.
128.ch: Country bands, trombone and city life
128.q: Music, yeah, all of them. Dance music. Played dances for people down there, Beurus, and all down there. Blue Connor. Poly Tom, you go all down there. Oh really? Poly Tom? Yeah, you go all down there, sure. Yeah.

306.t: Chris Kelly, Kid Rena's tone, and tailgate wagon battles
306.s: Rene calls Chris Kelly a country blues player, praises his brother's tone, and describes tailgate wagon contests between bands.
306.ch: Joe Rene: Lewis, the Rena band and New Orleans
306.q: No, he started out there in the country down the, like the fella said, down the bayou, yeah. So, he was mostly of a blues player. He was, he was, like this, what you call it, I would call it at that time, not a, a blues player, that's all we would say. Yes, yes. He could play blues, you know, he…

306.t: Economy Hall dances, his song, and a white cornetist; Chris's start on tin
306.s: Edna describes the hall and Chris's composed song for her, a white cornetist who played Chris's tunes, and how Chris began on a tin horn in the country.
306.q: The hall would be all lit up and the stand would be up like a grandstand, you know. The musicians would be up and the floor would be waxed. And the girls, the society girls, you know, would take the paper, you know, decorate it. It was beautiful. And have a police at the door at that time. What…

306.t: Musicians around Chris's band; George Lewis and Hank
306.s: Edna names musicians who came to the house, including Hank on bass and George Lewis on clarinet.
306.q: Mm-hmm. Uh, what do you remember about George Lewis? I remember he used to play clarinet.

306.t: Chris's favorite musicians and the music he liked
306.s: Edna says Chris favoured slow, soft music and lists old songs he played, and that he was liked by everyone.
306.q: And he was a popular man. Everybody liked him. He was a well-liked man.

871.t: Playing with Chris Kelly, the Blues King
871.s: About three or four years in Chris Kelly's band, whose members are named and which played mostly blues.
871.ch: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
871.q: Remember who was playing? Oh yeah, I can tell you. I can tell you. It just comes to my mind. Mealy Barnes was playing clarinet. You had Lawrence Marrera was playing banjo. Eddie Marrera, his brother, Lawrence's brother was playing bass. And Sonny Henry was playing trombone and I was playing drum.…

871.t: What made Chris Kelly's band stand out on the blues
871.s: Kelly played plunger-muted trumpet on Kelly's Love and the band had no printed arrangements.
871.ch: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
871.q: Well, we had a blues down there used to call it Keller's Love. And he was the only man that could play the Keller's Love. I mean, to suit the people, the puck. Because he used to use that wah-wah on his trumpet. And he used to say he was talking. Oh yeah. Did he use his hand or a plunger, a rubber…

871.t: Travel limits and the Black and Tan after Chris Kelly
871.s: With Kelly he stayed near home, then played the Black and Tan with Professor Mineta, Henry Martin and others.
871.ch: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
871.q: No, no. I mean we used to go from here to Bugalooza or over the lake like that, something like that, but never to go too far.

1000.t: Chris Kelly as the blues man; ear players versus readers
1000.s: Kelly played sad, varied blues that would still go over today; he compares ear players with reading musicians.
1000.q: But otherwise it would sound, it would take over so big if they was here, you know. Because these other fellows, like Pete Burkard, they was reading musicians. You know, they didn't get from here. They're just like a preacher. A preacher at that time was a better preacher than the preachers now for…

1000.t: Chris Kelly's mutes, plunger and derby, and long blues choruses
1000.s: Kelly used a plunger, wah-wah mute and derby, changed mutes between pieces, went out on open horn and played long blues that drew dancers.
1000.q: A plunger flusher, and he used a mute, wah-wah mute, and he used some other different mute. He had about four or five different mutes, and he used his derby. He had a derby, and he used his derby.

1000.t: Jobs with Chris Kelly and his band personnel
1000.s: He played house-dance jobs with Kelly's six-piece band and lists the banjo, guitar, piano and clarinet players Kelly used.
1000.q: Yes, I played a couple of jobs with Chris Kelly. There was a party, you know, house dancing. Used to have dances in the house, like you have a birthday party. Well, that would do your job too, you know, at that time. Because when people would give a birthday party, well, they'd use a band. And it…

886.t: Chris Kelly's band and George Popper
886.s: Playing with Chris Kelly, who paid well, and the pianist and trombone man George Popper.
886.q: How's the bond? You play a trombone. Mm-hm. money can't keep nobody. How's the bondage of their tram? You know the fat out of it, good tram. We talk good tram.

886.t: Chris Kelly's instrumentation, funeral and venues
886.s: Chris Kelly's banjo and bass players, his funeral, the halls he played and the size of his band.
886.q: And banjo, you know, he seemed to Chris could do the other band. Mm-hmm . Did he have a good funeral? Hmm? What kind of funeral did he have? What kind of funeral, man? He paid the Arnold back. Chris Keller, Sam Morgan, and Lorde Duran. He paid with the Arnold, Chris. Oh, man.

886.t: Dave Bailey, Mealy Barnes and clarinet players
886.s: Chris Kelly's drummer Dave Bailey, old-timer Mealy Barnes, and who played blues clarinet.
886.q: Where does Dave live now? I don't know where Dave's live. Somehow it's fun. But Dave really good trap drum, too. Dave is old, I'm telling you. Dave Bailey got a good age. Well, I'll have to dig up his address.

198.t: Cottrell, Chris Kelly, Kaiser, McCurtis and the Morgans
198.s: Barnes discusses Louis Cottrell with Kelly, Kelly's temper, and other clarinetists including Kaiser, Charlie McCurtis, Joe Watkins and Andrew Morgan.
198.q: So the band was Bush. Bush. And then my cousin Laura, Paul. Outside of that, I don't know. How about Louis Cotterall? Well, Louis Cotterall was actually a guy who was a musician.

198.t: Playing with Chris Kelly and the Johnny Brown band
198.s: Barnes talks about joining Kelly's band, its changing personnel, Johnny Brown's earlier band, and playing with Kelly before and after the Depression.
198.q: Well, after I got to Kelly, well I was probably stuck with Kelly, because he had lots of weight. And he was better than I was. I was getting plenty of weight myself, and I had a bar playing band, and we used to get lots of weight. Peter Patton, he would get plenty of weight too. Well, we had to,…

198.t: Chris Kelly's mutes and the band's ensemble style
198.s: Kelly used several small and rubber mutes, not bucket mutes. In the band he led the ensemble and Barnes played behind him.
198.q: He had, from a small mute. You know, Kelly had about four or five mutes. He didn't have no bucket mutes. Big mutes what they use now. But he had little mutes. They had a small mute and a rubber. And they put in a place like Kelly's Love and it blew it with it. Put that rubber on it. And that was…

896.t: Chris Kelly's band and why the banjo was never cut
896.s: After Carey he played with Chris Kelly and a few times with Kid Rene; Kelly's band had clarinet, trumpet and Chester on bass, and a seven-piece band was standard, always with banjo.
896.ch: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
896.q: After I left with Jack Carey and played with Chris Kelly a while. Played with him a while and then jumped around and played with Rene a couple of times.

896.t: Chris Kelly's jobs at the Bulls Club and in Mississippi
896.s: Kelly, Carey and Rene bands played the Bulls Club on 8th Street and towns in Mississippi such as Biloxi and McComb.
896.ch: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
896.q: On 8th Street. Played many times at that Bulls Club. Different bands played there many times. We played there. Played there several times with Jack and Chris Kelly and uh, and Rene at the Bulls. All right. And we used to go in Biloxi, Mississippi, and Peakyune, Mississippi, and Magnolia,…

896.t: Chris Kelly's trumpet style and plunger effects
896.s: Kelly was known for blues and a wah-wah effect using a toilet plunger in his trumpet, but could also play high notes and had a good range.
896.ch: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
896.q: Well, you know why they said Chris was very good on the blues? Chris was the first trumpet player that when they put out the Chalice Love, he took a toilet flush and made a wah-wah with that in his trumpet and everybody went wild. Not only the blues and the thing he played it was that.

177.s: He considers no one played the blues like Kelly, who used plumber's-plunger and derby mutes and drew crowds to fights; also Pork Chop Rag and High Society.
177.q: That's right, in the stand. He was a real blues man who really could mix him up. But there's none beat Chris Kelly. You like Chris Kelly. He was great. I wish they had some record of him. Yes, too bad. Yeah, he- I don't think it's another man born that may have it, could play the blues like him.…

177.t: Dance halls, advertising trucks, tailgate bucking, and Chris Kelly's blues
177.s: Jobs for bands like Rene's, Sunday tailgate competitions between bands, and why Chris Kelly was the greatest blues trumpeter.
177.q: jobs would a band like Rene play? Well he played advertisements, Sunday dances for clubs at home, and then he played clubs. Halls like the Corporators, Economy Hall, the Poitier Hall, the Jean-Amé Hall, the Fethian Tempher, all those old dance halls at that time. They had clubs mostly give dances,…

430.t: Chris Kelly and a prank at a lake picnic job
430.s: Asked about Chris Kelly, he recalls a picnic with Buddy Petit where guests tied the band's coats in knots.
430.q: That's a point on the story. That's a point on the story. That's a point on the story. I recall one time I played a pick-need with him.

430.t: Chris Kelly's death and Big Ike
430.s: Talk about when Chris Kelly died, his sharp dress, and a trombonist called Big Ike who killed a man.
430.q: Big Ike? Yeah, Big Ike, yeah. That's him? Yeah. Just like Chris Kelly. They said Chris Kelly had a lot of glow. All of his glow. All of his glow. Always smart. He's always smart. Did he wear expensive clothes? Well, he's a pretty neat guy. Don't make me terrible.

724.t: Chris Kelly as a blues trumpeter
724.s: He played one job with Kelly and praises his blues playing and mute work.
724.q: Well, Chris was, Chris was a real, he was good. He was strong. But I'll tell you one thing. There was nobody, there was nobody to play a blues like Chris. He was a blues man. You couldn't get him to beat him playing the blues. Charlie Lewis will tell you that same thing because George played with…

724.t: Louis Dumaine, Chris Kelly and Kid Thomas then and now
724.s: Never played with Dumaine, one job with Chris Kelly; Thomas's band hasn't changed.
724.q: What about Chris Kelly? Chris Kelly? I played one job with Chris Kelly. I don't remember where it was. All I remember is that I played one job with him. And Rene? You ever played with Rene? No, I never played with Rene. I never played with Rene. Well, I guess in those times you played one job with…

264.s: Chris Kelly as a well-liked blues player with a derby; Howard, once a drummer, learned from Chris.
264.q: Well, Chris Kelly was a great man. He was great. But I mean, he's not to comparison, you know, with Buddy, you know what I mean? And Chris had lots of jobs around here, because I worked with Chris Van a long time too. And he had plenty of jobs and people liked it, Chris. Chris was a well-liked man.…

264.t: Chris Kelly and Zardis's favorite trumpet players
264.s: Zardis worked with Chris Kelly and all the star trumpeters; he praises Rene and Petit and describes Kelly's hymn playing, plunger mute and foot beat.
264.q: Yes, I worked with Chris a long time. Yes, I worked with Chris Kelly a long time. I worked with all them big star trumpet players around here, all of them. All of them, yes sir.

775.t: Chris Kelly: knowing him in the country, his cornet and Kelly's Blues
775.s: Kelly was much older; he played a short cornet with mute and plunger, famously drawing a crowd with a blues played from the dance hall window.
775.ch: Chris Kelly and the country bands
775.q: Oh yeah he was way older than me. Yeah I remember him used to play. You know. I always say I wanted to be a musician. I used to follow him everywhere until I got big enough to learn how to play you see.

775.t: Personnel of Chris Kelly's country and city bands
775.s: He lists the Robinsons and others in Kelly's country band and the trombone, clarinet, bass and drums of his city band, with no piano.
775.ch: Chris Kelly and the country bands
775.q: Well, no. In the country, I couldn't exactly tell you who all, yeah I can tell you too who all was in the band or he's in the country. Jim Robinson. Jim Robinson was playing. Jim was everything down there. Yeah, Jim was playing uh, Ghetto. He used to get to all that time. And they had uh, Jim…

968.t: Playing with Sam Morgan, Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly
968.s: He recalls his brothers in Morgan's and Petit's bands, his own trips with them, and regular membership in Chris Kelly's band.
968.q: Well, Bill, I do remember him, he played with Sam Morgan's band. I remember that good, and Buddy Petit Band also. Simon and Joan was a member of the Buddy Petit Band, jazz band, and it was also myself I played with Buddy Petit.

968.t: Favorite trumpeters: Rene, Morgan and Chris Kelly on the corner
968.s: He compares Kid Rene, Sam Morgan and Chris Kelly, and describes bands meeting on the corner and Rene handling rivals.
968.q: Well uh, what was Cornette, that time Bill, Rene was the most jazzed man we had. I mean for fingering his corner and making those notes. And Sam Morgan was one of the sweetest trumpet players we had. But Chris Kelly, he had the ragged, ragged music you know, all the ragged music that people liked.…

282.t: The Deer Range band scatters after the levee break
282.s: The band members left Deer Range about when the levee broke and the plantation flooded; Ben Kelly is still alive in the area.
282.q: Yeah. And it didn't do any good to go around there because there wasn't nothing to do. No. All the plantation was under water. When the water did go into the, from the levee to the woods, well it just stayed there. And it got to be a real fish pond. Oh yeah. Yeah.

282.t: Chris Kelly in New Orleans and his blues
282.s: Ben never played much but Chris Kelly formed a band in the city; Brown played jobs with him, recalls the band's players and Kelly's blues.
282.q: Oh, Ben never did do much playing like Chris did. I didn't think so. No. After the brass band quit playing, well that was the end of Ben, you see? Yeah. There wasn't no more Ben, but Chris Kelly, he came here and he got organized and he got in a band playing around too.

570.t: After Buddy Petit died: joining Chris Kelly
570.s: The band fell apart without Petit, so Penn began playing with Chris Kelly, who also advertised in the streets.
570.q: Well, what happened to the band, we just played a while and didn't get much work. What we used to get when Buddy was living. So the men began to drop out. In fact, Buddy was well known and Buddy used to get plenty of work. So after he died, the fellas just dropped out and got in other different…

570.t: Sam Morgan, Celestin and the slapsticks
570.s: Sam Morgan and Celestin led the best bands; Penn thinks Chris Kelly started using slapsticks.
570.q: That was the first man started it. With them sticks. That was the first man started it. Then it's Celestine. You remember when Celestine had it.

127.s: Allen relays that Punch outplayed Kid Rena and Chris Kelly at Milneburg; Punch explains his 'runs' and clowning in blues playing.
127.q: Yeah, he'd run every Sunday everybody. And then the pavilion. And they were right close together, see. And I was so strong, you know, I was so loud. And the people over on the other pavilion, he was dancing by my music.

127.t: Chris Kelly, Ike Morgan and Punch's years in Chicago
127.s: Punch rates Chris Kelly above Sam Morgan and discusses Sam's brother Ike, whom he found sick on his return from Chicago.
127.q: Well yeah they was using second trumpet then but I'm on here You didn't know Ike? I've known him yeah but when I come back he was sick and never no good no more But he played second with his brother when I was in Chicago See I stayed in Chicago for 84 years Oh yeah that's right 84 years 84 years…

240.t: Chris Kelly, Bunk Johnson and playing with Ike Morgan in Mississippi towns
240.s: Asked about other trumpeters, he says he knew Chris Kelly and Bunk Johnson, whom he met in Iberia, and played with Sam Morgan's brother Isaiah around small Mississippi towns.
240.q: Oh, Chris Kelly, yes. Well, I just forgot the name of Bill. In those days I practically, I knew every guy, I knew every guy in those days that was playing and everything. And Bunk, oh, Bunk, you know, Bunk here, stop and he'd start over and he'd stop and he'd start over. But I knew Bunk and…

248.t: Chris Kelly's blues band and Kid Rene
248.s: Chris Kelly was the one blues band; Dawson played tenor banjo with him around 1912; Rene had the best band.
248.ch: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
248.q: Chris Kelly band was about the only band that used to play the blues All of them Practically everything he played sounded like the blues Yeah But he could blow, he could blow Yeah He could play it People was crazy about his band

868.t: Chris and Guy Kelly, Alexis Rochon and a tenor player
868.s: De De compares the Kelly brothers, Chris the any-job player and Guy the reader with Celestin, then names sax player Alexis Rochon.
868.q: Oh, they were two brothers, yeah, quite natural. But Guy Kelly, yeah, oh yeah, they were brothers. But Guy Kelly was more musical, you know, reading man. Read more. That's how he stayed more with Papa Celestine. But Chris was just actually anywhere, any little job, three pieces, four pieces, he…

175.s: Kelly was the favorite blues trumpeter, played growl with derby and plunger, and was heard at Economy Hall.
175.ch: Kid Rena, Kelly and the old trumpeters
175.q: Yes I remember a whole lot about Chris Kelly because he used to be the favorite blues trumpet player. I used to like to hear him play the blues more than anybody else. And I just imagine I could see him now playing the blues with perspiration just rolling off his forehead and everything like that.

176.t: Chris Kelly the blues man, mutes and high-note trumpeters
176.s: De De describes Chris Kelly as strictly a blues man whose playing could start fights, his plunger and tin-can mutes, and Albert Glenny working with him and Rene. Asked about high-note men, De De names Louis DeMaine.
176.ch: De De's career and trumpet players
176.q: Blues, strictly blues man. Nothing but blues. He was known to play more blues than any man in the city. He was known for that. He was known that Chris Kelly, if he wanted to- He was known for this one.

709.t: Chris's band members and his use of mutes
709.s: Jim Robinson played in the band, and Chris taught a former drummer, called Chita Howell in the transcript, to play trumpet. A clarinetist named Norwood quit. Chris started using mutes and plunger only after coming to the city, and crowds shouted 'preach'.
709.q: Jim Robinson. He played with him in the band. He had this boy, Chita Howell. He come up, Chris taught him he used to be a drummer. My brother broke him off the drum. Put him on a trumpet and made him famous during this time. Who was the clarinet player with the band? Do you remember who played…

179.t: Turtle Back Hall and Chris Kelly's seven-piece band
179.s: The Turtle Back (Young Men) Hall, where Chris Kelly played, and the quality of his seven-piece band.
179.q: Turtle Back back, yeah. That was the Young Men Hall. That's setback on Elmire and Lamarck.

253.t: Gigging with Jack Carey and Chris Kelly
253.s: Hall describes gigs with Jack Carey and Chris Kelly, their sidemen, and the Morgan brothers.
253.ch: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
253.q: Well, I worked with them for a while. I worked with Jack Carey for a while. Just like I was telling you, I worked with them on gigs, you know? Chris Kelly, I worked with them on gigs.

899.t: Pick-up work with Petit, Kelly, Celestin and the Young Tuxedo band
899.s: He subbed with Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly and Celestin, but his regular band was Cloverleaf; he replaced an ill drummer in the Young Tuxedo band for almost a year.
899.q: Well, I played in rake up bands like I played with Buddy Petit. I played with Chris Kelly. I played with Celestine too.

891.t: Chris Kelly's blues and his two-mute crying sound
891.s: Kelly was the strongest influence, a regular fellow who played blues; he combined a plunger-style flusher with a small mute to make the horn cry.
891.q: See, at that time, most of it was blues. And Chris Kelly was the man that looked like my ambition made me more on the trumpet, cause I always wanted to play the blues like him. And anywhere he would play, I mean the people, they said to say Chris was there and that was a lot of people, they said to…

773.t: Chris Kelly and the Parita and Rampart headquarters
773.s: Musicians like Chris Kelly gathered at Parita and Rampart to get jobs; Bob Lyon again.
773.q: Yeah, I remember him. Yeah, I hope to tell you. It was all kind of like right hand vows. You know, they had a certain bunch like Chris Kelly and all them boys. They're like, this was right together. Whenever you want them, all of them, you go right there, Parita and Ramport. They used to get all…

259.t: Chris Kelly's band and its clarinetists
259.s: Vincent says he played with Chris Kelly long before Mexico and recalls Kelly working him hard; he and Allen try to recall who played clarinet for Kelly.
259.q: He worked me out. He killed me from D to D to D. I didn't make a mistake. He told me to say why he got it. Ask him what tune that was. He said what tune was that? It was some wall. I can't think of it.

1040.t: Chris Kelly's blues cornet and Broussard's trumpet imitation
1040.s: Broussard describes Chris Kelly's soft blues playing, accompanying him on piano, and how it inspired his own vocal imitation of a trumpet.
1040.q: That's the trumpet player. He's the guy that was known for playing Kellis Love. That's the way I would tell him. He was one of the main elements at Jacob Melendez's party. Now, Chris Kelly was the guy. He could sit right here with that little short brass trumpet he had. Cornet. Cornet, yeah. That's…

262.t: The 1915 storm and playing with Chris Kelly
262.s: Bailey was with his brother's band at the 1915 storm, then six years with Kelly, including Tallulah.
262.ch: Young Tuxedo and Chris Kelly years
262.q: I was with my brother's band then. I had them. I was with Chris Kelly after that. But anyhow, I stayed with Chris Kelly after we stopped traveling, one, two, and all the different places. I played Chris Kelly six years. My brother, John, was in the band, so we played bass. We played together. Six…

251.t: Susquehanna boat to Mandeville and Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly
251.s: Albert worked on the Spanish Fort to Mandeville boat, befriended Buddy Petit, and praised Chris Kelly's tone and the dance hall balconies.
251.ch: Keyhole, comeback plans and old New Orleans players
251.q: Well I was a little too young to recall that. I was just a kid in my knee pants but I vividly recall running to the corner of my house when the parade would be coming. It would be just a band playing, ordinary street parade. And I just would stand up there and watch them. After I learned my horn…

271.t: Bands Leonce played with; the Christian swap
271.s: Leonce also worked with other bands, and Mello recalls a swap involving Charlie Christian and a disagreement with Jack Laine.
271.q: he worked with Galatay. He worked with Christian. He worked with Baraka. And he worked with Monjada, Triangle Officer. Which Monjada's in it? Sato. Sam. The clarinet player? I believe it is. And which Christian? Frank Christian played cornet. And Beans Christian, Emil, he played cornet. And who…

274.t: Mealy Barnes, Chris Kelly and Guy Kelly
274.s: Allen and Labat sort out whether Chris Kelly or Guy Kelly played with local bands.
274.q: Yeah, but Chris when he came there most of the time he was with Ellis. My mother's great. He's come out there most of the time he was with Ellis. My mother's great. Chris Kelly? I didn't know they played together. He's come out there most of the time he was with Ellis.

187.t: One bad job with Chris Kelly
187.s: Kelly paid him in whiskey bottles on a job in the district, and Nelson vowed never to work with him again.
187.q: I played with Chris Kelly, one job. One job, one job only, just one job, one night. Funny thing about it, I don't want to work with that fellow anymore.

713.t: Playing guitar and bass with Chris Kelly's band
713.s: Nelson recalls playing in Chris Kelly's band, where Johnny St. Cyr and Kid Rena were also heard; he names bassist Cleo and says he played guitar, banjo and some bass.
713.ch: Uncle Gaiye and New Orleans bands
713.q: Kelly that time oh you played with Chris yeah you remember who else was in the band oh let's see I can't think right now who always in the band I know we had a bass player named Cleo who was he used to change

121.t: Reviving the Dew Drop; Chris Kenner's key and fallen stars
121.s: Attendance rose when he arrived; wrong-key story with Chris Kenner, and stars who later came back down.
121.ch: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
121.q: Well, you know, attendance was why people had started going to other places. Because, you know, bad bands always run people. And so after I started playing there, the place came back up. And I stayed there so long. But I said that's why I got to know Frank Fairley well, you know, know where he was…

776.t: Charlie Creath's band on the St. Paul
776.s: Creath, a rhythm cornetist, led the St. Paul band to good business before leaving for Chicago.
776.q: Well Charlie Cedric was a cornet player and he specialized on rhythm. He really knew how to play the kind of music that the people wanted. He played on the St. Paul of St. Louis. He had, well the people, well the boat did a very nice business and was due to the fact that this fellow really put out,…

866.t: Chris Kelly band personnel, dance-hall jobs and instrumentation
866.s: Angrum names the drummer, guitarist and others who played with Kelly, and the dances and carnival jobs at the Italian hall on Esplanade. The band was seven pieces, with alto sax doubling clarinet.
866.q: Yeah. He had the music. Yeah, you know, but Chris had the music for it. Mm-hmm. Who else was in his band when you played with him? He had Red Happy, you know, he's dead too. Drummer. Drummer, yeah. I guess you heard of him. I never got to know him. Yeah. Big fella you call Ike. Big Ike Robinson.…

287.t: Chris Kelly the Blues King, and Buddy Petit's gift of a song
287.s: Morand played advertising jobs with Kelly, whom no band could touch with his blues. Buddy Petit gave him the song later recorded by the Harlem Hamfats.
287.q: I used to play with Chris Kelly on many advertising. He's known as the Blues King. And no band couldn't touch him on the street. When he'd get his rubber flush out and start wow-waring the blues, that was all. He'd run Lewis. And then at that time, people was crazy about blues in the Orleans.

847.t: Riding the trucks and handing out handbills
847.s: He rode trucks handing out handbills while trumpeters like Chris Kelly and Buddy Petit played, but cannot recall their sidemen.
847.ch: Early New Orleans drummers and bands
847.q: That was my trumpet player. I used to love to hear him play trumpet. Him and Chris Kelly and Buddy P.T. Those who were trumpet players I used to get on the truck. When they would be playing on the truck I would hop on the truck and ride around. Listen to them. They didn't mind you getting on the…

633.t: Chris Kelly double-booking jobs and sending substitutes
633.s: Kelly took deposits on two jobs and sent a substitute trumpeter, which disgusted Barnes.
633.q: Well he'd pick up just who he could get, what he could, somebody he could cheat. See, he'd take, he'd take that job, he'd be done, got, I'd be done, get him a deposit on a job, you know. And he'd take another job, you see. And he'd take another band and get a trumpet player and send with me.…

1041.t: Sam Morgan's advice, Chris Kelly, and Joyce McCullen's orchestra
1041.s: Sam Morgan encouraged him and he took over from a drummer to play with Chris Kelly at the Bulls Club for about three years, then with McCullen's orchestra.
1041.q: So, Morgan, Sam Morgan's come by every night. He said, boy you're going to be a good drummer someday. He said, now you should show me how to put that left foot and right foot down and keep the time with the music. So after a while, Morgan needed a drummer. Well he'd take me to the boy, just like I…

571.t: Chris Kelly's mute and the tunes he played
571.s: Talk about how Chris Kelly played with a silver mute and a plunger, and about recorded versions of his tunes.
571.q: Well, she has a love with one of his tunes. Uh, and we were like, oh, when I... Uh, Mr. Galga, Mr. Sheen. What's up? Galga, Mr. Sheen. Come out in the early twas. Mr. Galga, Mr. Sheen. Um, Black Snake Rouge. He's like, Mary. Yeah, they have a girl. And a lot of old standards. But he clearly knows.…

192.t: Drummers Happy and Faso, and Chris Kelly and Sam Morgan bands
192.s: He praises Happy and Faso, then recalls playing with Chris Kelly's band and compares it with Sam Morgan's.
192.q: next man next time was Zuta Singleton the jazz band Zuta Singleton we had another drummer what gave me a whole lot of ideas in the jazz band with Chris Kelly and that was Faso

290.t: Chris Kelly and filling his jobs
290.s: He played jobs for Chris Kelly when Kelly was double-booked; Kelly did not read.
290.ch: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
290.q: Oh yeah, yeah, I know Chris Kelly, I know him good. I played quite a few jobs for him. Now let me explain what I mean by for him. I'm playing with my own band, see, and he's got two jobs, and he's got to get rid of one in some kind of way, because he can't play with one. So several times I went on…

291.t: Working with Chris Kelly's band and clarinetist Emile
291.s: He worked with Chris Kelly's band without being a regular and says Emile was its clarinetist, never changed and never played saxophone.
291.q: Yeah. Yeah. That was his regular climbing player. Yeah. Sometime I would work with him on the, with the Alphurs Sax. Yeah.

139.t: Fish fry rules, parade bands, Chris Kelly, Celestin and a medicine show
139.s: Miller finishes on fish fries, police warnings and fines, then recalls parade bands, Chris Kelly's plunger mute, Celestin's band, singers like Bessie Smith, Robichaux, and touring with Earl Foster's medicine show.
139.q: 12-inch records, big, big records, those large records. The big horn and all, some of them. The horn sticking out on the victuals and all of them. In other words, some of them would stand the victual and wind the victuals, every day they had no piano. Yeah. And a lot of times, guys like I said…

573.t: Chris Kelly and playing the Mississippi coast
573.s: Kelly didn't come over the coast; Sam's reputation opened Pass Christian jobs for Morgan's band.
573.ch: Playing New Orleans and the coast
573.q: He didn't, he didn't used to come over there. The fellas used to, was in that, was in power, them was old Foster, Foster, Foster, Foster and his brother.

638.t: Chris Kelly's shifting personnel and trumpet style
638.s: Kelly's bands changed constantly; Kid Howard played most like Chris Kelly.
638.q: Well, Chris been dead a long time. Yeah. And I played with him. Chris knew they were all different fellas. That's the point. He never did have no, none of them had no straight up band, honey. Yeah. They always changed it, man. Because if you got a job for Saturday, and I got a job, and then you…

766.t: Chris Kelly and his blues playing
766.s: Milton left Kelly's band after a couple of jobs; Kelly played blues with a hat or plunger mute.
766.q: I played with Chris Kelly a couple of jobs, I mean. But I left him. I mean, I didn't like his ways. I left him. I didn't stay with him.

849.t: Chris Kelly, his trombonist, and cousin Pratt's bands and death
849.s: He recalls Kelly playing Going Back to Jamaica, his trombonist, low pay of the era, and Pratt dying in 1947.
849.q: But never got the hearing, though. They played. Man, I used to like to hear that man playing Going Back to Jamaica. He had one of those short... My cousin was playing with him, didn't he? This wasn't a great picture. Playing Going Back to Jamaica. Man, that man could make the horn talk. Going…

1.t: Chris Kelly, who never read music, and the Mobile trips
1.s: Danny says plenty of New Orleans players couldn't read, and Chris Kelly was a great blues trumpeter whose plunger work impressed Mobile musicians.
1.ch: A musical family and the old New Orleans bands
1.q: Now, they had just loads of musicians in New Orleans who couldn't play no music. They was all saying, "Nobody pay you to read no music; they pay you to play!"
